lesson.title: The Second Derivative: Curvature, Concavity, and Acceleration
lesson.summary: The second derivative measures how a rate of change is itself changing, which translates directly into two of the most useful readings in calculus: the acceleration of a moving object and the concavity of a curve.
lesson.body:
As the previous chapter established, f''(x) is just f'(x) differentiated one more time. What makes it worth singling out is the double layer of meaning it carries. If f'(x) measures how fast something is changing, then f''(x) measures how fast that rate of change is itself changing, a rate of a rate.

In physics, if s(t) gives the position of an object at time t, then s'(t) = v(t) is its velocity, and s''(t) = v'(t) = a(t) is its acceleration. As a worked example, let s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t, position in meters with t in seconds. Then v(t) = s'(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9, and a(t) = s''(t) = 6t - 12. At t = 2 seconds, a(2) = 6(2) - 12 = 0, so the acceleration momentarily vanishes right at the instant the velocity reaches a local extreme, since a = v' is exactly what controls where v is increasing or decreasing.

Graphically, the sign of f''(x) tells you which way a curve bends. Where f''(x) > 0, the graph is concave up, bending like a cup, with tangent lines sitting below the curve. Where f''(x) < 0, the graph is concave down, bending like a cap, with tangent lines sitting above the curve. As a worked example, let f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2. Then f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x and f''(x) = 6x - 6, which is zero at x = 1. For x < 1, f''(x) < 0, so the graph is concave down; for x > 1, f''(x) > 0, so it is concave up. The point (1, f(1)) = (1, -2) is where the concavity switches, called an inflection point.

Acceleration is literally the second derivative of position, and concavity is literally the sign of the second derivative of any function's graph, so this one higher order derivative unifies a physics idea and a geometry idea under a single piece of notation, f''(x) or d^2y/dx^2, which is exactly why the higher order derivative framework from the previous chapter earns its place in the toolkit.
